label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong, Monday, June 21, 1926.

label: text
text: AN HISTORICAL SOCIETY

label: text
text: There may be a comparative handful of people in the Colony to-day who will participate in the celebrations of the centenary of Hongkong fifteen years hence. Three years hence Western Australia will complete the first century of her existence as a unit of the British Empire. In this connection, according to the West Australian, the most powerful newspaper in that State, the Premier has initiated a project to collect all available old prints and photographs of historical interest, to be published as a pictorial record of a century's endeavour. This step moves our contemporary to remark: "There is not in our midst a public body whose primary interest lies in the recording of the intensely interesting local history of the State. We lack an Historical Society."

label: text
text: Although Hongkong's centenary is much further off, the same plea could be made even now for the establishment of an Historical Society. How often has it been deplored that with the passing of the old "China hands" there are also irretrievably passing fragments, pages, chapters of our local history and social development? Outside of scanty and sporadic newspaper contributions the bulk of this information goes with the actors in our daily drama. Whose work is it to collect and preserve these records while there is the opportunity?—no one's as yet, but with an Historical Society in active existence a treasure house would exist, full of informative memoirs of those who in their varied ways have built up the Colony to what it is to-day. Father Time works unceasingly and too easily does his erasing hand move the events of the past into oblivion. The present year has witnessed the retirement for good of a large number of old residents, whilst others have passed away—few of them leaving behind (If Sir Paul Chatter be excepted) much of a tangible nature, on which to lay the foundation of an Historical Society.

label: text
text: An Historical Society, with enthusiastic working members throughout the Colony, would effectively circumvent Time, the obliterator, by causing to be written up the episodes and encouraging the collection of the stories of those who recollect something of what has been—those “good old, days” in Hongkong of which we still hear something. With research articles, reminiscences, Government records, old prints, and photographs, how much of the past could be preserved!

label: text
text: The idea is not new. The language of this plea is not original. But that cannot discount the immense value of an Historical Society to the Colony. Let it not be said of Hongkong, as it is now being said of Western Australia, that three years before our centenary there is to be deplored the lack of an Historical Society. Such

label: text
text: a body cannot fail to be of the greatest interest during the stay here of every present British resident, whilst it would be performing an incalculably useful service to the Colony in the years after the great majority of us have departed for good to other climes. We may not have a centenary nearly due to act as an incentive to form an Historical Society, but we do have the lesson of Western Australia before us, and we surely can profit therefrom!

label: paragraph_title
text: 14,000 MILES.

label: paragraph_title
text: BRITISH AIRMEN BACK HOME TO-DAY.

label: text
text: FLIGHT ENDED.

label: text
text: Rugby; June 20.

label: text
text: A proposal that the four Royal Air Force machines which are expected to reach England to-morrow, on the completion of the 14,000 miles flight to South Africa, should alight on the Thames at Westminster, has not been favoured by the Air Ministry for technical seasons. The airmen will alight at Lee Solent as arranged. Their maes will have the floats removed prior to their participation on July 3 in the annual Air Force pageant at Hendon. On that occasion about 180 air craft drawn from the Home Defence Army co-operation and training units will take part, including 16 new machines of a fresh type.

label: paragraph_title
text: FRENCH CRISIS.

label: text
text: Squadron air drill, to be carried out by wireless telephony, orders being given by the Squadron Leader from his machine in the air or from the wireless ground station, will be one of the features of the display.—British Wireless Service.

label: text
text: Penang, June 11.—The death occurred at the General Hospital last night of Mr. William E. Felgate, late of Taiping. The deceased as a planter was well-known in Kedah, F.M.S. and Johore. The funeral took place this afternoon.

label: paragraph_title
text:
BRIAND AT THE HELM
AGAIN.

label: text
text: M. HERRIOT'S FAILURE.

label: text
text: Paris, June 19.

label: text
text: An American visitor, after hearing M. Poincare speak about inter-Allied debts at a country ceremony, sent him $10,000 towards the "Save the France Fund," and stipulated that his name should not be disclosed.

label: text
text: M. Herriot will inform the President that he is unable to form a Cabinet owing to the difficulties encountered.—Reuter's Service.

label: text
text: M. Herriot has abandoned his task of form a Cabinet, and M. Briand has been re-summoned.

label: text
text: M. Herriot's failure to form a Cabinet was due to the inability of members of the intended Cabinet to agree with regard to the financial policy.

label: text
text:
After informing M. Doumergue, the President, this morning of his inability to form a Cabinet, M. Horriot declared he had formed a plan for financial rehabilitation, permitting "simplication of" the system of taxation and reduction of excessive taxes, but setting aside for the sinking fund exceptional resources such as inherited or acquired wealth. He conferred all night long with different members of the prospective Cabinet, but following several refusals of portfolios, he finally gave up the task.
M. Briand has agreed to form a Cabinet.—Reuter's Service.

label: text
text: After consulting with M. Briand, M. Painleve spoke optimistically of M. Briand's chances of success, but thought that the Cabinet would not be completed till tomorrow.—Reuter's Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: Briand's Plan.

label: text
text: That the idea of forming a Cabinet of the National Union was abandoned as impossible was mentioned by M. Briand in an interview, though he intimated his desire of giving the new Cabinet the broadest possible basis. He intends in the first place to invite the support of the bloc National by offering M. Poincare a portfolio.

label: paragraph_title
text: TACNA-ARICA.

label: paragraph_title
text:
AWAITING ARBITRATION
EFFECTS.

label: paragraph_title
text: Washington, June 19.

label: text
text: President Coolidge believes that the American Government can do nothing towards adjusting the Tacna-Arica dispute until the effect on recent developments of arbitration and mediation negotiations can be determined.—Reuter's American Service.

label: text
text:
Boran Into Fray.
Washington, June 19.

label: text
text: Senator Borah has entered the Tacna-Arica dispute, announcing after a long conversation with Senhor Allesandri, the ex-President of Chile, he "told the ex-President the only thing that interested me was to know how the United States could get out of the Tacna-Arica problem with "honour." — Reuter's American Service.

label: text
text: [American representatives reported that it was impossible to submit the Tacna-Aricn dispute to arbitration owing to the failure of Chile to provide guarantees for Peruvian voters. Chile's counter proposals and Mr. Kellogg's suggestion to divide Tacna-Arics so as to afford Bolivia an outlet to the sea were rejected by Peru. Chile, after failure of further proposals whereby a smaller portion of the disputed territory should be handed over to Peru, announced her intention of resuming military occupation. Strong guards were posted outside the houses of American Commissioners.]

label: paragraph_title
text: DR. COLE.

label: paragraph_title
text:
DEPARTATION ORDER
REVOKED:

label: text
text: Mexico City, June 19.

label: text
text: President Calles has revoked the deportation of Dr. Cole, It having been proved that he was ignorant of violating the law relating to Insurance Companies. — Reuter's American Service.

label: text
text: [A previous cable stated:—The Mexican authorities have ordered the deportation of a Canadian doctor, named William Cole, who has been practising at Torreon for 16 years. Cole appeared in the local Court and secured a stay of execution for 72 hours. The British Vice-Consul at Torreon has telegraphed to the British Minister in Mexico city, drawing attention to the case and assuring him that Cole is an honourable man, and declaring that the deportation order should be revoked. The official explanation of the deporting of Dr. Cole says he was guilty of violation of the recent Insurance Law by acting as medical examiner to insurance companies which had not complied with the law.]

label: paragraph_title
text: CATHOLIC CONGRESS

label: text
text: GREAT WELCOME TO ELEVEN CARDINALS.

label: text
text: PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE.

label: text
text: Chicago, June 19th

label: text
text: A welcoming assemblage of 14,000 packed the Coliseum, the City's largest auditorium, when Cardinal Bonzano and other distinguished ecclesiastics to the Eucharistic Congress came on to the platform.

label: text
text:
The outstanding feature was a message from President Coolidge, delivered by the Secretary of Labour, Mr. Davis, who had specially come from Washington.
The President declared the United States had long been under the imputation of putting too much emphasis upon material things. "Perhaps we have been subject to that kind of criticism not so much because we really are more interested in material prosperity than others, but because in that direction we have been more successful than others."

label: text
text: The President argued that material prosperity could not be secured unless it rested upon spiritual realities, all business being founded on mutual good faith, as indeed all modern Governments were.

label: text
text: Mr. Davis pleaded on his own account for religious tolerance, and was tumultuously applauded when he said: "If there is any anti-Catholic prejudice in America it comes from persons who make a speciality of prejudice." — Reuter's American Service.

label: text
text:
Amid “unsurpassed scenes of stately splendour the International Eucharistic Congress was formally opened by the celebration of Pontifical High Mass in the presence of eleven Cardinals and upward of six thousand people.
Masses were celebrated in the Churches in the Archdiocese of Chicago.

label: text
text: Pilgrims from all nations joined in the spiritual bouquet of a million Communions, promised to the Pope by Cardinal Mundelein, Archbishop of Chicago.—Reuter's American Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: Delegates Suspect.

label: text
text: Out of 77 jugo-slav delegates to the Eucharistic Congress 64 have been detained and ordered to proceed to Ellis Island for examination. It is officially stated that the authorities are not satisfied that the delegates, who are all laymen, come to the United States solely to attend the Congress.

label: paragraph_title
text:
LIQUOR LAWS.
THE CANADIAN CUSTOMS SCANDAL.

label: text
text: Ottawa. June 19.

label: text
text: Sweeping recommendations in favour of the dismissal or suspension of certain officials in Montreal and other Quebec ports of entry, the retirement of a number of high officials in Montreal, and the stiffening of the preventive service and prohibition of clearances on liquor vessels from Canadian ports for the United States and "Rum Row" are contained in the report of the House of Commons Committee.

label: text
text: The Committee also recommend prosecutions for the recovery of moneys from a long list of companies found to have evaded the Customs and excise laws. Reference is made to the "slowly degenerating efficiency" of the Customs Department in recent years, and the ex-Minister of the Bureau is criticised.

label: text
text:
The Committee find there is some presumption that a proportion of liquor, allegedly consigned from Canada for foreign ports and cleared without payment of excise on sales and tax, returns to Canada for consumption.
The tightening up of regulations by the imposition of taxes on all liquor released from bond or entering in bond is recommended and also a reduction of the ports of entry, which are 681, as compared with 270 in the United States and 80 in Great Britain.—Reuter's American Service.

text: MEXICAN OIL.

label: paragraph_title
text: AMERICAN TO CONFER WITH PRESIDENT.

label: text
text: The prominent New York business man, Mr. Henry Doherty, has arrived. It is suggested he is desircus of conferring with President Calles in connection with the development of Government oil lands.—Reuter's American Service.

text: LORD WILLINGDON

label: paragraph_title
text:
LEAVES PEKING FOR HOME
VIA SIBERIA

label: text
text: Lord and Lady Willingdon left Peking this afternoon by special train for Tientsin, whence they leave for Europe via Siberia.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: COAL CRISIS.

label: text
text: GOVERNMENT'S EIGHT-HOUR BILL

label: text
text: TO BE RUSHED THROUGH.

label: paragraph_title
text: Rugby, Juno 20.

label: text
text: The new Bill enabling a return to the eight-hours working day in the coal industry will be formally introduced in the House of Commons to-morrow, and the Government intends to pass it through all its Parliamentary stages as rapidly as possible.

label: text
text: The measure does not repeal the Seven Hours Act, but merely suspends it for a period which has not yet been defined, but which will be announced to-morrow. It will probably be from three to five years.

label: text
text: The Government also intends to pass into law before the Recess a second Bill incorporating measures of reorganisation in the industry.—British Wireless Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: SOVIET'S MISTAKE.

label: paragraph_title
text: WARNINGS FROM BRITISH STATESMEN.

label: text
text: Strong references to Russia were uttered by Ministers in speeches to-day.

label: text
text: Mr. Winston Churchill, in London, spoke of the Soviet's mistake in thinking the "same sort of stuff with which they bamboozled the moujiks would suit Britain." He was of the opinion that the United States policy to Russia was right as was proved by the fact that without in the slightest way countenancing Bolshevik principles, they had done more trade with Russia than we.

label: text
text:
Mr. Churchill warned the people against lending money to Russia, and that the British Government would not accept responsibility if they were defrauded. He advised traders to get payment or full security before despatching goods.
Lord Birkenhead, at Luton, declared that nobody was deceived by the protestations of Moscow that the Russian Government was not behind the money forwarded for the alleged purpose of alleviating distress in the coalfields, and concluded that unless we observe signs of change it will be necessary to decide whether we should retain any degree of association with a country whose avowed purpose, known to the whole world, is to undermine the historical greatness of Britain.—Reuter's Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: FLOWING GOLD.

label: paragraph_title
text:
AMERICA'S SURPLUS STILL CROWING.
Washington June 10

label: text
text:
It is indicated by the Treasury that the Government surplus for the current fiscal year has been increased to over $300,000,000 owing to the large amount of income tax collected in the present quarter.—

Reuter's American Service.

label: paragraph_title
text:
APPOINTMENTS OF VICE-
MINISTERS.

label: text
text:
Peking, June 19.
It is unofficially stated that the Cabinet will meet on Monday in order to consider and promulgate Vice-Ministers' appointments.

label: text
text: It will meet again on Tuesday to draft a telegram urging Wu Pei-fu and Chang Tso-lin to come to Peking as soon as possible in order to discuss the question of political reorganisation. — Reuter's Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: AEROPLANE CRASH.

label: paragraph_title
text:
STRIKES MAST OF TORPEDO
BOAT.

label: text
text: A French pilot was killed in an extraordinary accident.

label: text
text: A French naval aeroplane engaged in a practice flight, rose over the Harbour and struck the mast of an American torpedo boat. The plane crashed to the deck of the vessel and fell into the sea. —Reuter's Service.

label: text
text: Manila, June 9.—The death rate from certain diseases in Manila, the only city in the islands with all sanitary conveniences, is altogether too high, in the opinion of many health officers.

label: text
text: According to Dr. H. Larn, senior surgeon and diagnostician of the Philippine health service, Manila during the last three years registered 816 dysentery deaths.

label: text
text: During the same period, he points out, there were 1,823 deaths of intestinal diseases and enteritis in the city. The city's toll from typhoid amounted to 1,051 lives. Naglected cases, according to Dr. Lara, is the reason behind this condition. For instance, he says, cases of dysenteries in Manila, for many years, have not been regularly reported.
